passage: Vishal had already typed three paragraphs to his manager, Usha, explaining why he should not present the quarterly review to the client. The client deserved a senior voice. His numbers needed another week. The team would benefit from hearing someone new. In the office pantry, waiting for the kettle, he peeled off a sticky note and wrote the reason without polish: I'm scared I'll freeze in front of them. Seven words. He reread the email and asked himself: if his friend Rohit sent him this, would he buy it? He could hear his own reply: "You're nervous, yaar, just say so." Vishal deleted two paragraphs, then the third. The new message was one line: "Honestly, I'm nervous about presenting. Could we do a practice run first?" Usha answered in ten minutes; she had already booked the small conference room for Thursday. "Of course. 4 pm. 🙂"

qa.q: What did Vishal write on the sticky note?
qa.a: I'm scared I'll freeze in front of them.

qa.q: Why did the three-paragraph email feel reasonable to Vishal while he was writing it?
qa.a: Every reason sounded mature and focused on the client and the team, so it let him avoid the less flattering truth that he was afraid of freezing.

qa.q: Which choice turned things around for Vishal, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking whether he would accept the same email from Rohit; he knew he wouldn't, so he sent the honest one-line version and got the practice run he actually needed.

qa.q: What might Usha have done if she had received the original three paragraphs?
qa.a: She might simply have handed the presentation to someone else, never learning that Vishal was nervous or that a practice run could help him.

grounding: An adult writes down the short, honest reason for dodging a presentation and tests his long email against what he would accept from a friend.

passage:
Dear Parul,
Last week I sent you a long message about why I can't move into the flat with you: the commute, the rent split, my "need for a quiet workspace". This morning I did something odd. I wrote the real reason on the back of an electricity bill, and it came out in one sentence: I'm afraid that if we live together, you'll see how messy and moody I get, and you'll like me less.
Then I asked myself: if you had sent me my message, would I have believed it? No. You've known me since we were two girls sharing one lab stool, and your mother still calls me her second daughter. I'd have noticed the commute is twenty minutes, and I'd have called you.
So here is the shorter version, and it isn't flattering. I'm still not sure about moving in, but I'd rather decide it with you honestly than hide behind rent maths.
Can we talk on Sunday?
Love,
Vasudha

qa.q: Where did Vasudha write the real reason?
qa.a: On the back of an electricity bill.

qa.q: What was Vasudha worried about underneath the talk of commute and rent?
qa.a: She feared that living together would show Parul how messy and moody she gets, and that Parul would like her less; the practical reasons felt safer to say.

qa.q: What choice in the letter changes the direction of the conversation?
qa.a: Admitting the one-sentence reason instead of repeating the rent maths, which gives Parul something real to answer so they can decide together.

qa.q: How might Parul feel reading this letter after the first long message?
qa.a: Parul may feel relieved and trusted, because the first message left her guessing, while this one shows a worry she can actually respond to.

grounding: An adult writes out the honest reason for turning down a friend's offer to share a flat, finds it shorter and less flattering, and checks whether she would believe her own excuse.

passage: Okay, Gopika, since you keep asking. Last month I told everyone I skipped the design fellowship because the stipend was too low and my mother needs me close by. All true-ish. Then one night I tried something my cousin swears by: take a blank page, write the reason, and imagine a friend saying it to you. I wrote, "The stipend is low and Amma needs me." Then I imagined you giving me that same excuse. I'd have laughed: "Your mother is fine, she goes to yoga more than you do." And the same is true of mine. So I wrote again, slower. The second line was, "Forty people applied last year, and I didn't want to be one of the thirty-five who got rejected." That's it. Not noble at all. Kind of embarrassing, honestly. But at least now I know what I'm actually deciding about. The next round closes in March. I've started the portfolio. So yes, this is Sangeeta, applying again. Don't tell anyone yet.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta first write as the reason for skipping the fellowship?
qa.a: The stipend is low and Amma needs me.

qa.q: Why did the stipend-and-Amma reason feel convincing to Sangeeta at first?
qa.a: Both parts were partly true and made the choice sound responsible, which hid the fear of rejection that was harder to admit.

qa.q: Which step helped Sangeeta find the real reason, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Imagining Gopika giving the same excuse; Sangeeta knew it wouldn't pass, wrote the honest line about rejection, and started a portfolio for March.

qa.q: What can Gopika understand now that the stipend story hid?
qa.a: Gopika can see that fear of rejection, not money or family, held Sangeeta back, so Gopika can encourage the application instead of arguing about stipends.

grounding: An adult imagines a friend offering the same polished excuse, then writes down the shorter and less flattering reason underneath it: fear of rejection.

passage:
I'm Mohit, and I share a flat in Andheri with Divyansh. For a week he had been explaining why he wasn't applying for the Singapore posting his firm had offered: the humidity, his mother's knees, the role "wasn't really strategic", a better opening might come next year. Each version was longer than the last.
On Sunday night I found him at the dining table with an index card. He wrote one line, covered it with his hand, then looked up. "Mohit, if I heard all those reasons from you, would I believe them?"
"Honestly? No."
He turned the card over. It said: I'm scared I'll be out of my depth there.
Nine words. He stared at it a long time. I don't know everything he felt, but his shoulders dropped, as if something heavy had been set down. On Monday he booked a call with the manager who'd offered the role, to ask what support new people got.

qa.q: What did Divyansh write on the index card?
qa.a: I'm scared I'll be out of my depth there.

qa.q: Why might the long list of reasons have felt more comfortable to Divyansh than the one line?
qa.a: The humidity, his mother's knees and next year made staying back sound sensible and even caring; the single line admitted fear, which is less flattering, so facing it took effort but brought relief.

qa.q: What turning point came from testing the excuse?
qa.a: Once the real reason was named as fear, Divyansh could act on it, booking a call to ask what support new people got instead of hiding behind the weather and next year.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Mohit to be asked, "would I believe them?"
qa.a: Mohit had to choose between being polite and being honest; answering "No" risked stinging a friend, but it gave Divyansh the push to turn the card over.

grounding: Shows, through a flatmate's eyes, an adult who writes the real reason for a choice and checks it against what they would accept from a friend, finding it short and unflattering.

passage:
Sunday. Swati texted her cousin Yogesh that she couldn't make his housewarming in Nashik. "Train timings are awful, I've got a deadline, and I think a cold is coming." She added a sad face and felt oddly pleased with how reasonable it sounded.
Tuesday. Clearing her desk, Swati found the message still open. She tried a trick her flatmate used: if Yogesh sent me these three reasons, would I buy them? No. She'd call it an excuse. So she opened the notes on her phone and typed the actual reason. Neha will be there, and I still owe her an apology. One line. Not flattering at all.
Friday. She called Yogesh. "The cold was an excuse. It's Neha. I've been avoiding her since last year."
Yogesh was quiet, then laughed softly. "Come anyway. I'll put you two on chai duty."
She booked the early train that night.

qa.q: What three reasons did Swati give Yogesh on Sunday?
qa.a: Train timings were awful, she had a deadline, and she thought a cold was coming.

qa.q: Why did the three reasons feel convincing to Swati at first?
qa.a: Each was partly true and made her sound busy and sensible, which kept her away from the less flattering truth that she was avoiding Neha.

qa.q: What test helped Swati see past her own excuse?
qa.a: Asking whether she would accept the same three reasons from Yogesh; when she knew she wouldn't, she typed the short, real reason and could act on it 🙂

qa.q: How might Yogesh have felt hearing the real reason on the phone?
qa.a: Yogesh might feel trusted and closer to Swati, and glad to know the true problem so he could help, instead of feeling brushed off with train timings.

grounding: Illustrates an adult who writes down the real reason for skipping a family event, tests her excuse against what she'd accept from someone else, and finds the honest reason shorter and less flattering.

passage: Jomon, you've written a page of reasons for missing the team dinner. Let your old Vinita akka tell you a trick I learnt. When I was twenty-five, in Kottayam, my closest friend Leena got engaged, and I didn't go to the function. I told her it was a work deadline, my scooter was being repaired, my mother needed me. A long, clever list. That night I sat with a notebook and wrote one line: the real reason. It was, "I'm jealous she's getting married first." Short. Ugly. Then I asked myself, if Leena gave me that list of excuses, would I believe her? No. I'd know something was hiding under it. So the next morning I went to her house with sweets, and I told her the short version. She laughed and cried. We're still friends. So, Jomon: what's your one line?

qa.q: What did young Vinita write as the real reason?
qa.a: "I'm jealous she's getting married first."

qa.q: Why did the short reason feel ugly to young Vinita?
qa.a: It was honest and unflattering; admitting jealousy made her feel ashamed, while the long list had made her look busy and responsible.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking whether she'd believe the same list from Leena; seeing she wouldn't made her go with sweets and tell the truth, which saved the friendship.

qa.q: How might Leena have felt hearing the short version?
qa.a: Leena probably felt surprised, a bit hurt, and touched by the honesty, which is why she laughed and cried.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, writing down the real reason for a choice and testing an excuse by asking if a friend's version would be accepted.

passage: Ten minutes before the deadline, Aadhya was still typing her email to Ganga, the team lead, explaining why she couldn't run Friday's client workshop. The office was noisy, the fan rattled, and her draft had grown to nine lines: a clash with another meeting, slides not ready, a possible cold, the client preferring someone senior. She stopped. On a sticky note she wrote the real reason, just for herself: "I'm scared of presenting to twelve people." She looked at it, then at the email. If a friend sent Ganga that nine-line email, would Aadhya believe it? No. She'd think, something's up. With four minutes left, she deleted the draft and typed: "Ganga, honestly, presenting to a big room makes me nervous. Could I co-run it with you this time?" She hit send before she could change it. Ganga replied in a minute: "Yes. Proud of you for asking."

qa.q: How many lines had Aadhya's draft grown to?
qa.a: Nine lines.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya write the real reason on a sticky note first?
qa.a: She felt anxious and a little ashamed, and writing it privately let her face the honest reason before deciding what to send.

qa.q: What test did Aadhya use, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She asked whether she would believe the nine-line email from a friend, which showed her the long excuse would look like it was hiding something.

qa.q: How might Ganga see the short, honest email?
qa.a: Ganga seems pleased and proud, glad to get a clear request instead of a list of excuses.

grounding: Shows an adult writing down the real reason for a choice and testing the excuse against what a friend's version would sound like, under time pressure.

passage: In his Kolkata flat, Madhav had a long message ready for his sister Bidisha: he couldn't come to her dance recital on Saturday because of a work presentation, and traffic, and the recital running late, and his back. He read it over and felt uneasy. So he did what he'd started doing lately. He opened his notes and wrote, "Real reason:" and waited. It came out small. "Baba will be there, and I don't want to face him after our fight." He stared at it. If Bidisha sent him that long list of excuses, would he accept it? He'd know she was avoiding something. The honest reason was shorter and made him look worse. He deleted the long message. He called her instead. "I'll come. But sit me away from Baba, okay?" Bidisha was quiet, then said, "Okay. Thank you for coming."

qa.q: Who was dancing in the recital on Saturday?
qa.a: His sister Bidisha.

qa.q: Why did Madhav feel uneasy reading his long message?
qa.a: He sensed the list of reasons was covering something, and felt uncomfortable because the real reason made him look worse.

qa.q: What makes Madhav's "Real reason:" note a useful habit?
qa.a: Writing the honest reason and asking if he'd accept the excuse from Bidisha helped him see what the long list hid and choose better.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel when Madhav calls instead of texting excuses?
qa.a: Bidisha seems moved and grateful that he is coming and being honest about Baba.

grounding: Shows an adult writing down the real reason for a choice and testing the excuse by imagining it from his sister, finding the honest reason shorter and less flattering.

passage:
"Okay, final list," Mahima said, tapping the notebook with a pen. "One, a deadline on Monday. Two, the train is at six in the morning. Three, the hall is miles from the station. Four, I went to the last family function."
Keerthana looked up from her laptop. "That's a lot of reasons for skipping one engagement."
"They're all true."
"Sure. If I read you that list about my cousin's function, would you believe me?"
Mahima opened her mouth. Closed it. "I'd think you were hiding something."
"So?"
Mahima crossed out all four and wrote one line underneath. She turned the notebook round: I don't want Periamma asking why I'm still not married.
"Oof," Keerthana said softly. "That one I believe."
"It's shorter," Mahima said. "And uglier." She sighed. "Maybe I go, and leave early."

qa.q: How many reasons were on Mahima's first list?
qa.a: Mahima's list had four reasons: the Monday deadline, the six o'clock train, the far hall and the last family function.

qa.q: Why did the four reasons feel convincing to Mahima at first?
qa.a: Mahima was anxious about Periamma's marriage questions, and the practical reasons hid that uncomfortable feeling behind respectable ones.

qa.q: Which test helped Mahima, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether the same list from a friend would be believable showed the reasons were covering something, and the honest line led to a better plan.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see the new line in the notebook?
qa.a: Keerthana finds it believable and feels for Mahima, since it is short and plainly honest.

grounding: Shows an adult who writes the real reason for skipping a family engagement and tests her excuses as if a friend had given them.

passage:
I'm Dhruv, and last spring I dropped out of a Saturday pottery class after four weeks. To Jasleen I gave a whole speech: the studio was too far, the clay was poor, the teacher never explained glazing, and honestly my Saturdays needed rest. It sounded very mature.

That night I tried something from a book. I wrote the real reason on a sticky note, then asked myself whether I'd accept my speech from Jasleen. I wouldn't. I'd say, "You sound like you're defending a case."

The sticky note said: Everyone else's bowls stand up. Mine collapse. I feel stupid.

Ten words, and not flattering at all. But it was something I could actually work with. I emailed the teacher, asked for help with centring the clay, and went back the next Saturday.

qa.q: After how many weeks did Dhruv drop out of the pottery class?
qa.a: Dhruv dropped out after four weeks.

qa.q: What feeling was hiding under Dhruv's speech to Jasleen?
qa.a: Dhruv felt embarrassed and stupid because the bowls kept collapsing, and the mature-sounding reasons covered that shame.

qa.q: Which step helped Dhruv go back, and why?
qa.a: Writing the real reason and asking whether the same speech from Jasleen would be accepted exposed the excuse, and the honest reason pointed to a fix: asking the teacher for help.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have heard the speech about the studio?
qa.a: Jasleen may have nodded along but also sensed it sounded like a case being defended rather than the real story.

grounding: An adult looks back on writing down the real, unflattering reason for quitting a class and testing the excuse against a friend's.

passage:
Supervision note, field office, 14 June.

Leela told me this morning she wants to withdraw from presenting at the district health meeting. She gave five reasons: the slides aren't final, travel clashes with survey work, a senior colleague could present better, the data is from only two villages, and the meeting is "mostly a formality anyway".

I did not argue with any of them. I asked her to write the one real reason on a separate sheet, and then to read her five reasons as if her friend Rukmini had said them. She laughed. "I'd tell Rukmini she was scared."

The sheet said: "I'm afraid they'll ask a question I can't answer." Much shorter.

We agreed she will present, and we will practise likely questions together on Thursday. I'll sit in the front row.

Aparna, programme supervisor

qa.q: How many reasons did Leela give for withdrawing?
qa.a: Leela gave five reasons.

qa.q: Why might the five reasons feel sensible to Leela?
qa.a: Leela is afraid of a question she can't answer, and the practical reasons let her dodge that fear while still sounding responsible.

qa.q: What did Aparna's approach get right?
qa.a: Aparna didn't argue, asked for the one real reason and the friend test, and then planned practice for likely questions.

qa.q: What would change if Rukmini had given Leela the same five reasons?
qa.a: Leela would see through them at once and call Rukmini scared, which is exactly the test that exposed Leela's own excuse.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a young worker writing down the real reason for withdrawing and judging her excuses as a friend's.

passage:
Saturday night.
Skipped Shalini's birthday dinner. My message to her said: "So sorry, massive work deadline, and my stomach's been off, and the traffic to Andheri is insane on Saturdays." Three reasons. Very convincing. Then I did the thing I've been practising: I wrote the real reason in my notebook, the way I'd say it to myself. It was one line. "I didn't want to see her college friends, because they make me feel boring." Then I asked: if Shalini sent me my own message, would I believe it? No. I'd think, three excuses means none of them is the real one. Ugh. So tomorrow I'm calling her to say sorry, properly, and maybe tell her the true thing, gently.
Vasudha

qa.q: How many reasons did Vasudha's message give?
qa.a: Three: a work deadline, an upset stomach, and the traffic to Andheri.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel on writing down the real reason?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and a bit embarrassed, because the honest reason, feeling boring around the college friends, was short and unflattering.

qa.q: What test did Vasudha use, and why does it work?
qa.a: Writing the real reason and asking whether Vasudha would believe the same message from Shalini; it shows a stack of excuses up as a cover.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel getting the three-reason message?
qa.a: She might feel a little let down and unsure which reason was the real one.

grounding: An adult writes down the real, shorter reason behind an excuse and tests it by asking whether a friend's version would convince.

passage: Rajni had missed the parents' meeting at the village school, and on the walk home past the mustard fields she practised her explanation for the headmistress: the bus was late, her mother needed her, the rain had made the path muddy. It sounded smooth. Then she stopped at the well and did what her aunt had taught her. She said the real reason aloud, in one sentence. "I was afraid of Gopal's father shouting again." Short. Unflattering. True. Then she asked herself: if Disha, my colleague, gave me the three-part version, would I believe her? No. The next morning Rajni told the headmistress the truth and asked if Disha could sit with her at the next meeting.

qa.q: Where did Rajni stop to think?
qa.a: At the well.

qa.q: What was Rajni actually feeling about the meeting?
qa.a: She was afraid of Gopal's father shouting again.

qa.a: Saying the real reason in one sentence and asking whether she would believe Disha's three-part version; it led her to tell the truth and ask for support.

grounding: An adult tests a smooth excuse by stating the real reason in one sentence and asking whether she would accept the excuse from a colleague.

passage:
Liam had told three people why he'd dropped out of the Tuesday Spanish class in Dublin: the bus timetable was awful, the teacher moved too fast, and with work, who had the energy? The reasons sounded solid every time.
On Sunday, tidying his desk, he found the course book and, half as a joke, wrote the reasons on a sticky note. Then he asked himself: if Yosef said this to me, would I buy it? He crossed out the bus; there was one every ten minutes. He crossed out the teacher. Underneath he wrote the real reason: "I felt stupid when I couldn't answer in front of everyone." One short line, and not flattering.
He texted Yosef, who had signed up with him: "Actually, I quit because I was embarrassed. Could we practise together before class?"

qa.q: What did Liam first write on the sticky note?
qa.a: His reasons for dropping the class: the bus timetable, the teacher moving too fast, and having no energy after work.

qa.q: Why had the long list of reasons felt convincing to Liam?
qa.a: They protected him from feeling embarrassed; the real reason, feeling stupid in front of everyone, was less flattering and harder to admit.

qa.q: What made Liam's test work?
qa.a: Imagining Yosef giving the same excuses made the weak ones obvious, and the honest one-line reason pointed to a real fix: practising together 🙂.

qa.q: How might Yosef react to Liam's text?
qa.a: Yosef may feel trusted and glad to help, and might find it easier to admit his own struggles in class too.

grounding: An adult writes down the reasons for a choice, tests them as if a friend gave them, and finds the short, unflattering real reason.
